Charles Hamilton recorded in considerable detail a variety of activities associated with mercantile enterprises in Charleston during the 1870s.
Descriptive elements abound and give the viewer some idea of the lively street life in Charleston's downtown area.
None

After being seriously injured in an accident as an 11-year-old boy, Joseph Stock was encouraged to study art. With help from his family and a specially designed wheelchair, Stock traveled widely and developed a successful career as a portraitist. Appealing portraits of children were among his specialties.

Hicks painted several versions of George Washington's famous winter journey across the Delaware River. Two of the earliest were signboards commissioned for both sides of the bridge at the site of Washington's original crossing. Hicks admired the general's leadership and wrote about the significance of his role in the War for Independence.
According to the inscription in the lower left, Hicks produced this painting for Newtown physician and dentist Maurice P. Linton, the son of a friend and fellow soldier.
"Painted by Edw. Hicks in the 69th year of his age/for Doctor M. Linton of Newtown, son of his/old Friend & fellow Soldier, James Linton."
It likely was painted as payment for a medical bill.

In this famous scene, Hicks painted most of the Declaration of Independence signers with similar and stylized faces. However, he attempted to individualize the more important members of the drafting committee, including Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin, who stand at the table.
Hicks presented this picture to his son, Isaac Worstall Hicks, and it remained in his family for two generations.

One of Hicks's favorite subjects was the 1682 meeting between prominent Quaker William Penn and the Lenni-Lenape Indians.
This event was significant for Pennsylvania Quakers because it represented Penn's dream of a peaceful society free of religious persecution.
Hicks created more than a dozen versions of this scene and often included it in the background of his Peaceable Kingdom paintings. He varied the details and arrangements, but elements such as the large tree, boats on the river, and background buildings are present in each painting.

In his role as a minister, Hicks devoted long periods of time to travel, often at great distance. In 1819-1820, he journeyed to New York and lower Canada where he attended several dozen
Quaker meetings. During this trip, Hicks visited Niagara Falls, a site he regarded as an inspiration of God's handiwork. He later featured the natural wonder in some of his paintings.
This fireboard, a painting on wood used to hide the empty fireplace during summer, was created for Dr. Joseph Parrish of Philadelphia, likely in appreciation for services the physician provided for free.

At an early age, Hicks was sent by his father to live with family friends, David and Elizabeth Twining. The local Quaker couple raised Edward along with their four daughters. For the rest of his life, Hicks recalled the comfort, love, and security he experienced in the Twining household. Almost 60 years later, he painted a memory that depicts himself as a young boy, standing at his foster mother's knee.
Hicks completed four versions of this scene, most likely giving a canvas to each of the Twining daughters, Sarah, Elizabeth, Mary, and Beulah.

Over the years Hicks completed nearly 130 paintings depicting farm scenes, historical and religious subjects, and patriotic images. This is the last painting created before his death and is arguably his finest work. It is the summation of its predecessors, combining the artist's remarkable skill, his love of family and friends, and his innate Quaker values for order, simplicity, and man's good works on earth. In short, this painting is a highly personal statement about the serenity Hicks fervently desired for humanity, and for his step-brother and friend, David Leedom, who commissioned the work.

This portrait of America's most beloved folk artist was rendered by the subject's cousin, Thomas Hicks. He captured the older painter in a familiar pose, the composition showing him in the process of creating a version of his favorite subject, the Peaceable Kingdom.
Thomas painted the canvas while he was an apprentice in his cousin's sign and carriage painting shop. The younger man executed a number of portraits during this time. In 1839, he left to study art in Philadelphia, ultimately becoming a well-respected and skilled portraitist and landscape painter.

Edward Hicks painted the creatures in this portrait of James
C. Cornell's prize bull with more finesse and sophistication than the flat, linear, and stylized animals seen in his most well-known works, dispelling any notion of his inability to paint academically.
Hicks's acceptance of this commission and subsequent payment by the bull's owner was unusual, suggesting that the artist may have reconciled his life-long struggle between his vocation as a painter and his religious faith, which denounced pictorial art.

Hicks created more than 60 variations of the Peaceable Kingdom. A group of his early works features a painted border inscribed with the biblical passage from Isaiah 11:6-9. The verse was the foundation of all Hicks's Peaceable Kingdom paintings, and he used the religious message to convey his concerns about contemporary affairs within the Society of Friends.

As Hicks continued to paint new versions of the Peaceable Kingdom, he began adding a background scene of Quaker William Penn and the local Pennsylvania Indians. Hicks admired Penn for his good relationship with the Lenni-Lenape and considered the Quaker's fair and honest communications a fulfillment of God's peaceable kingdom on earth.
Hicks used his training as a sign, coach, and decorative painter to create the lettering and decorative corner blocks in the border of this painting. More than a dozen versions of these paintings include these skillful designs.

During the early 1830s, Hicks began rearranging the figures in his Peaceable Kingdom paintings to reflect his anguish over the 1827 division of the Society of Friends into the two Hicksite and Orthodox factions. He no longer wholly relied on printed sources for his compositions; instead Hicks's canvases evolved into personal statements that became entirely his own in concept and design.
Hicks removed symbols such as the grapevine that were associated with Holy Communion and Orthodox Quakerism.
He replaced them with sheaves of wheat and ears of corn that better represented fellow Hicksite Quaker beliefs of salvation through the "light within."

During the 1840s, Hicks altered his compositions again to include more animals in a variety of arrangements. The two leopards in this painting - one submissive and the other aggressive - likely represent his acknowledgment of the difficulty of attaining peace between the two Quaker factions. Leopards also symbolized a
love of excitement that conflicted with Quaker codes of simplicity, restraint, and plainness, again illustrating discord and strife among Friends members.
Joseph Watson, a fellow Hicksite Quaker from nearby Langhorne, Pennsylvania, commissioned this painting. Hicks gifted the majority of his Peaceable Kingdom paintings to Quakers who shared his religious views.

An example of a side-wheeler steamboat, the Enoch Dean was built by Benjamin C. Terry of Keyport New Jersey, in 1852. That same year the steamboat was painted by the prolific ship painter James Bard. Prior to the Civil War, the Enoch Dean ran from New York City on the East River to Flushing and College Point on Long Island. Bard's placement of the steamboat between a threatening sky and stylized waves serves as a reminder of the time when America's rivers were her great highways.
he Enoch Dean was employed by the Union during the Civil War as a cargo ship. A notice appeared in the New York Herald on May 6th of 1865 which described her final voyage.
"Steamer Enoch Dean, Hallett, from Savannah 19th ult., for the islands lying [south] of Savannah, with freedmen and their families, farming utensils, etc., while passing through a creek emptying into St. Catherine's Sound, struck a snag and sunk."

James Bard and his twin brother, John, rank among America's most acclaimed painters of steamboats and small sailing vessels. Although the brothers collaborated on about two dozen pictures, most Bard works are signed or attributed to James alone. James is known to have completed three portraits of the schooner William Bayles, two in 1854 and another in
1860. The commissioners of all three paintings remain unknown but both 1854 versions bear the sail maker's name on the mainsails.
he William Bayles was a 67 ton schooner built in  Nyack, New York in 1853 by John B. Voriz
Although the schooner changed owners, masters and home ports several times throughout her life, it is thought that one of her first contracts was hauling stone from a Tarrytown quarry to New York City. The William Bayles operated out of the port of New York until 1862, after which she is listed as serving out of various ports in Connecticut, New Hampshire and finally Massachusetts, from whence she was reported
"lost at sea" in March of 1874.

The first international yacht exposition was launched in England in 1851, marking the first formal racing competition between British and American vessels. On August 22 of that year, the schooner America became the first winner in the 53-mile contest around England's Isle of Wight. To mark the occasion, the Royal Yacht Squadron's trophy was thereafter known as the America's Cup.
Weighing in at 179 tons, the America was built in the spring of 1851 to the design specifications of Manhattan shipbuilder George Steers and financed by a syndicate under the leadership of John Cox Stevens, one of the founders of the New York Yacht Club. Following her racing career, the schooner sailed for both the North and the South during the Civil War. She was then presented to the United States Naval Academy in 1921 and served the Navy until an accident lead to her demise during World War II.

The brig Georgiana was built in 1827 in Duxbury Massachusetts, and owned by Frederick W. racy of Boston. By 1845, William Crispin was captain of the vessel which was registered in Boston. In January of 1847, the Georgiana, was reported in a New Orleans paper as being in Tampico, Mexico, as part of the United States-Mexican War that lasted from 1846-1848.
James Cuy Evans created this portrait of the Georgiana
in 1846 likely before the ship set sail for Mexico.
Evans was born in New York City and worked as a shoemaker before enlisting in the U.S. Marine Corps in 1829. After his military career, he settled in New Orleans, where he worked as a painter from 1846 to
1859. He advertised that he and his partner did house, ship and sign painting as well as historical, marine and ornamental painting. The careful execution of the complex network of ropes, chains and other lines comprising the rigging of the Georgiana speak to Evan's skill as a ship painter. A full-rigged ship of this size could have upwards of two hundred principal lines, whose name and function each crewman needed to know, and whose timely adjustments could save a mast in a storm or catch the faintest breeze in calm waters.

Piece Title: Chestina Farley and a Favored Kitten
Plaque Description:
This portrait of Chestina Farley with her kitten was commissioned by her father, George Porterfield Farley, a planter, and his wife, Charlotte, in the late 1840s. The Farleys were descendants of the earliest settlers to Jefferson County, Mississippi, and lived in an area known as Shankstown (now Lorman). Raised as Catholics, Chestina and her two sisters, Charlotte and Georgia, were educated in Bardstown, Kentucky, at Nazareth Academy, a boarding school operated by the Sisters of Charity.
Thomas Poindexter painted portraits of the three Farley sisters not long after he arrived in Mississippi. Originally from Kentucky, he spent time in Tennessee before moving his family to Hind County, Mississippi, prior to 1850. Poindexter's travels through these states are well documented by local newspapers advertising his services as a portrait painter.
None

Female sitters wear similar attire in many of Ammi Philip's
portraits created within the same time frame. Such repetition suited the speedy, self-assured, and highly-graphic style the artist began to develop in the 1820s, although the wording of an 1809 advertisement suggests that he touted aspects of the practice from the beginning. In that notice, he offered to show women in "elegant dresses in the prevailing fashion of the day," seemingly claiming that, on canvas, he could embellish, update, or perhaps even totally
replace the apparel his sitters wore if they so
desired. The idea might have appealed to fashion-conscious females, but for Phillips, the primary allure was speed and, thus, profit.
Earlier owners of the portrait recorded the sitter's name as "Mrs.
H. B. Van Rensselaer of Kinderhook, 1820," but records reveal no woman with these initials. It is possible that "H. B." was confused for "H. P." If this identification is correct then Jane was in her twenties when her portrait was completed, and by 1825 had five children.

These charming portraits likely depict artist James Herring and his first wife, Ann. Although neither includes a formal signature, one of the books depicted in the back of the male sitter's portrait includes the title The Life of J. Herring. Both portraits are marked on the back with the date "January 1823" and while such a book did not exist in 1823, in 1863, Herring published an autobiography recording his family history and career.
In 1838, Herring set out to establish an arts organization focused on spreading national awareness of American arts through the distribution of etchings, medals, and an illustrated newsletter.
The initial exhibition of The American Art-Union, held that year, included a "Portrait of J. Herring, by himself" among the 260 works exhibited.

This portrait was signed by "R. B. Crafft," who appears in other records as Resin B. Craft, Reasoner Crafft, and R. B. Crofft.
Born in Ohio, he was first noted as a portraitist in Fort Wayne, Indiana. This 1836 likeness of an unidentified merchant, one of his earliest canvases, may well show a Fort Wayne citizen. Crafft also worked in Kentucky, lowa, and Ohio, and portraits of a Mississippi couple suggest he worked there as well.
While the swagged drapery and realistic modeling of the merchant's face indicate a degree of familiarity with artistic conventions, the irregularities in perspective seen in the
fingers, the relationship of the ledger and desk, and the row of tilted account books suggest the hand of an artist struggling to solve technical problems in his own way.
None

The striking unity of this large and complex family portrait speaks to the talent of artist Jefferson Gaunt, and perhaps to the close connections between the sibling subjects. Every child is depicted physically connected to or overlapping another. They are the eight children of William and Maria Antoinette Jennison. William was a prosperous merchant who brought his family from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to Brooklyn, New York, by 1832.
Less than a year after this portrait was completed, Melinda Anna, the girl in the yellow dress, died. Her brother Charles the boy with the hoop on the far right) became a successful merchant.
It was through his family that the portrait descended to the donor.
Gauntt was an artist with academic aspirations. His work was exhibited at the Philadelphia Academy of Fine Arts and the
National Academy of Design in New York City. Despite his formal training, Gaunt's composition exhibits a slight awkwardness in execution, but that does not diminish the warmth and appeal of the Jennison children and their pet birds.

This portrait is often thought to typify stern, humorless New Englanders. But records reveal that New Englanders could be as light-hearted and fun-loving as people in any other region of America. Indeed, the fact that Calvin Hall (1759-1833)
commissioned a life-size, full-length portrait of his daughter suggests that he was a particularly indulgent, doting father. Hall's own half-length likeness and that of his wife Mercy Barnes Hall presumably reflect his and painter James Brown's mutual goal of images that conveyed simple dignity. Such a depiction suited a Revolutionary War veteran like Hall, who fought in New York State.
The background of the portrait is believed to show part of Cheshire, Massachusetts,
including the tavern built by Hall and a partner in 1804. The building, which still stands, housed prisoners during the War of 1812.

John Bradley immigrated to America about 1826, previously having lived and painted in Suffolk, England. Little is known of his early life and training. On several of his American portraits he inscribed his name and the words "from Great Britton," implying that he took pride in his origin and perhaps hoped his British background would appeal to customers.
The boy's rather stiff position on the edge of his seat suggests
His eagerness to finish posing. A silver-headed child-sized
walking stick and an elegant black-embroidered coat reflect his parents' affluence, while their attention to his education is confirmed by the copy of The History of Robin Hood in his hand.

Family tradition credits Captain James Smith (1762-1818) with having painted this group portrait of his extended family.
He included himself, in profile, at the upper right. In 1790, the Scottish sea captain and merchant settled in Dumfries, Prince William County, Virginia, where he and his family lived on a 600-acre estate called Cedar Grove. A decline in the local shipping industry forced Smith into bankruptcy and relocation. In 1806, he opened a store in Richmond, and his family joined him there the next year.
This portrait is thought to have been painted around the time of their reunion.
Smith's unusual composition spotlights his wife, Rachel King Smith (1774-1825). She is surrounded by five of their nine children as well as her mother Rachel Westwood King McClurg.
The artist included a profile of himself in the far upper right. The two miniatures probably represent members of Rachel's extended family, William and Mary Tabb Westwood of Briarfields in Hampton, Virginia.

The beautiful inscription on the back of the painting to the left was written by the artist who described himself as a "Professor of Penmanship." In the self-portrait seen above, Arnold depicts himself with quill in hand. This highly ornamented miniature, which likely doubled as an advertisement for his work, was created almost 10 years before his portrait of Mary Mattingly. Note that at the bottom, almost lost in the details of his pen, he states his career as a "Portrait and Miniature Painter."

Piece Title: Jane Payne, Archer Payne, and Martha Payne
Plaque Description:
New research identifies the artist of these three portraits as William Hodgson, a London carver and painter.178
Hodgson announced his arrival in Richmond advertising his services as a limner who under "very moderate terms" produced various sizes of "portrait[s] in oil" from full-length likenesses to portrait miniatures. Arguably Hodgson's most notable commission was fulfilled for Archer Payne, Sr. (1748-1831), and his wife, Martha Dandridge Payne (1748-1791), who lived at New Market plantation in Goochland County, Virginia. The Paynes were portrayed along with their nine surviving children, three of whom are shown here. Archer Jr. (b. 1775) is seen in the center flanked by two of his sisters, Jane
(b. 1778/9) and Martha (b. 1773) with her cat. Their mother, Martha, was the granddaughter of Alexander Spotswood, governor of Virginia from 1710-1722.
The frames on all three likenesses are original and most likely, locally made. Unlike their urban counterparts, these simple, black molded profiles rest directly on the surface of the picture where they are nailed through the front of the canvas onto the painting's wooden stretchers. This unusual method of framing deviates from standard practice where the artwork would attach to the frame from the back, underscoring the rural production of these works and the problem-solving ability of this artist.

This portrait of a young gentleman has long been identified as
Daniel Clarke. Several men of that name and the appropriate
age lived in the region where itinerant folk artist Jacob Frymire worked. The well-dressed subject sits before a red drapery that lifts to reveal a substantial brick dwelling. These elements imply that the subject was economically successful.
Jacob Frymire is estimated to have completed over 200 portraits, largely of middle income sitters in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Kentucky. By 1794, he was working as an itinerant painter, sometimes rendering portraits for innkeepers in exchange for his board. Later in life, Frymire kept a "Painting Room" on King Street in Shippensburg, Pennsylvania. After he inherited his father's substantial land holdings in 1816, the artist gradually turned his focus to his farm and family. He died in 1822.

Artists did not always sign their works, but a distinctive style or key traits repeated in several paintings may suggest that the same person created all of them. When this occurs,
researchers often assign the unidentified artist a title so that his or her body of work is recognized. Twenty portraits are attributed to the artist who depicted Mrs. Seth Wilkinson, and because her likeness was among the first studied, her name became the title for the maker. The word "limner" means "painter."
Circumstantial evidence suggests that the Wilkinson Limner started painting while serving a sentence for counterfeiting at the state prison in Charlestown, Massachusetts. About 1827, he began creating more luxurious settings for his sitters; Mrs.
Wilkinson's rich surroundings reflect the new trend. It was recorded that Mrs. Wilkinson married the captain of a New York fire brigade, but, like her artist, her history remains elusive.

While the United States was not involved in any active military conflict during the 1830s, state militia regiments kept busy with drills, parades, and musters. The uniformed subject of this portrait proudly stands before what is likely an encampment of the New York State Militia, an annual occurrence for most state units.
The likeness of Major General Whitaker may have been painted by British-born John Bradley, an artist then working in New York.
Bradley advertised his skills as a portrait painter in New York
City directories from 1836 to 1847, but portraits like this one rendered from outside the city suggest he also traveled to gain commissions.

Eleazer Bullard (1787-1858) commissioned Erastus Salisbury
Field to paint these companion portraits of himself and his second wife about 1835. At the same time, Bullard had Field
paint portraits of his daughter from his
first marriage and son-in-law, Mrs. and Mr. Squire Brewer. All four paintings are the same size and carry identical frames so that they may hang as a group. The couples even share the same poses.
Field began painting in 1825 and by the 1830s had developed
an efficient style that allowed him to complete a half-length portrait in a day, for which he charged $4.00. His basic format could be modified to suit his clients. In this instance, Eleazer is portrayed leaning on a table with an inkwell and quill while Emily rests her arm on a table with a pincushion.

Piece Title: John H Pardee and Elbert A Pardee
Plaque Description:
An accident crippled Joseph Whiting Stock when he was eleven years old. Nevertheless, with encouragement and help from his family and his physician (who designed
a special wheelchair for him, he developed a successful career as a portraitist. He not only maintained a studio in Springfield, Massachusetts, but also traveled widely in New England and upstate New York, by coach and train. The subjects of this double portrait were the first children born to John Alling Pardee and his wife, Jeanette R. Hotchkiss.
The couple lived in New Haven, Connecticut, where John's occupation was reported variously as a "joiner," "master carpenter," and "house joiner."
In his journal, Stock recorded charging $20 for the boys' portrait and $10 apiece for individual likenesses of their parents. Stock's journal also noted that he stayed with the family for a week while he painted them.

Piece Title: Anna Webster Worthington Bull and her Daughter
Plaque Description: None

William Matthew Prior's depictions of children rank among his most engaging efforts, and this ambitiously composed, large-scale painting is one of his best. Pets appear in many youngsters' likenesses, but few paintings so successfully capture the special bond between children and animals. The long yellow feather in the girl's hand reveals that Prior has interrupted a moment of lighthearted play shared by child and cat.
As evidenced here, Prior
Mastered sophisticated
painting techniques. Yet
throughout his career, he continued to offer flatly-painted portraits, like the adjacent likeness of Phebe Ann
Hawes that incorporated minimal modeling. This was done by simplifying or eliminating the subtle transitions between lights and darks
The Artist as a Young Man: Self Portrait
Fenimore Art Museum
used to produce the convincing illusion of three-dimensional form on a two-dimensional surface. Because such works could be executed more rapidly, they cost less and, therefore, appealed to a far greater range of clients.

This portrait exemplifies William Matthew Prior's flat portraiture or, as he phrased it, "without shade or shadow." For such works, he first painted the head and hair, then suggested clothing and backgrounds with broad, sweeping brushstrokes, finally picking out facial features and other details with a small, pointed brush. The results were strikingly decorative. Thanks to the artist's knack for capturing personal characteristics, his portraits also succeeded as credible likenesses.
Phebe Ann Carlton (1822-1881) was born in Frankfort, Maine, and married Philander Hawes there on October 26, 1843. The couple, who had four children, are thought to have lived their entire lives in Maine. It is unclear whether they traveled to Prior's post-1840 home base in Boston or whether Prior traveled to their locale. The latter possibility is suggested by a gap in the artist's Boston advertisements.

Piece Title: Jonathan Adams Bartlett and Harriet Glines
Plaque Description:
Jonathan Bartlett's self-portrait provides a rare glimpse of a folk artist’s conception of himself and his vocation, just as it documents the tools, of his trade. Artistic pride is evident in the prominent display of brushes, palette, palette knife, grinding slab, and muller, the cone-shaped device shown resting on the slab, used to crush dry pigment. Although clearly proud of his artistic
abilities, Barlett (1817-1902) was a farmer and house carpenter by trade and also tried his hand at cabinetmaking, photography, music, and teaching. The original mahogany-veneered frames were reportedly made by him.
The painter signed dated this companion portrait of his fiancée, Harriet A. Glines (1818-1893), whom he married in May 1842. The couple raised eight children plus three grandchildren left motherless by early deaths in the family. The Bartletts' portraits descended in their family until 1976.
None

Piece Title: Polsapianna Bull Dorr and Maria Ester Dorr
Plaque Description:
The pastel background of this portrait is characteristic of Phillip’s so-called “Border Period,” when he frequented
communities on either side of the western Massachusetts-eastern New York boundary. The modeling of these early figures is unrealistically conceived and painstakingly applied, suggesting the artist's struggle to teach himself the rudiments of effectively representing three-dimensional forms.
Three children were born to Polsapianna Bull (783-1869) and Russel Dor after Philips
painted the family's nine members in 1814- 1815. Thus Polsapianna was left with the task of raising ten children aged fifteen months to twenty years when her husband died prematurely in 1824. Despite the fact that Polsapianna never remarried, she managed to see her six daughters wed to prosperous men, while three of her sons became lawyers and one a doctor. Judging by Maria Esther's apparent infancy, one assumes the group of Dorr family portraits to have been painted within the year following her birth on April 16, 1814.
None

William Anderson Roberts was a prolific artist who painted in North Carolina, Virginia, and Kentucky beginning about
1857. He fought with the Confederate Army during the Civil War, but resumed his artistic activity at the war's conclusion.
Roberts's appointment books record roughly 106 portraits completed in Caswell County, his North Carolina home. There he painted several members of the extended Russell family.
Among the wealthiest residents of the county, they were well positioned geographically and financially to be Roberts's patrons. The youthful subjects of this painting, Annie "Fannie" Elizabeth Russell (1864-1955), left, and her older sister, Sarah Bell (1862-1886), were born to William Russell and Martha Jane Womack. Their portrait was most likely completed in early 1866, shortly before the death of their father.

Many of the mission churches in what is now New Mexico were richly decorated with "santos" or devotional images. The paintings and sculptures depicted religious subjects and were often used for worship or religious observances. This "retablo" or panel painting depicts San Longinos, the legendary Roman soldier who was instantly converted to Christianity after he pierced Christ's side with a lance at the crucifixion. It belongs to a body of work widely recognized as the first folk art created in New Mexico.
The artist is sometimes also known as the Truchas Master, named for the church and town where the majority of his works were found.
None

R. A. Miller began painting and drawing after deteriorating eyesight forced him to retire from full-time work. Since age 12, he held a variety of jobs on a farm, in a cotton mill, and at a nearby gas station, but none were as impactful as his role of a Free Will Baptist minister. Faith played an important part in Miller's life, motivating him to create visual messages of God's word.
The Bible served as inspiration for much of Miller's work and devils were a common subject. He drew the demons in various sizes and forms on a wide array of found materials such as scrap metal and wood, often characterizing each figure's temperament by a specific color. According to Miller, the red and purple devils shown here are the
type "that get you in all kind of trouble." Miller's colorful artwork gained considerable notoriety after being featured in a 1984 music video for the rock band R.E.M.

Self-taught artist Malcah Zeldis (born Mildred Brightman in 1931 in the Bronx, New York) was encouraged to pursue painting as a young woman, but did not begin her artistic work in earnest until her 50s.
Her version of the "Peaceable Kingdom," an American folk art composition most notably associated with Edward Hicks, places a human twist on the harmonious landscape. Zeldis populates her painting with pivotal historical and contemporary personages. She states that "summoning" these individuals brought her great pleasure and creativity, "as though [these figures] imparted their strength to me." In this composition, Zeldis summoned diverse notables including Eleanor Roosevelt, Luciano Pavarotti, Nelson Mandela, her parents, Abraham Lincoln, Martin Luther King, Louis Armstrong, and Charlie Chaplin.

Henry Church (1836-1908) worked as a blacksmith in Chagrin Falls, Ohio. Other talents included painting, drawing, and wood and stone carving. An original and independent thinker, Church prepared for death by carving his own memorial stone (in the shape of a lion).
The artist's reasons for executing this lively painting remain speculative, but many scholars believe it was intended as a spoof on the uninspired, time-worn Victorian tabletop settings. Church's playful rendition with the two rambunctious monkeys and aggravated policeman is a favorite with museum visitors. He apparently patterned his monkeys from an 1890s trade advertisement showing two monkeys fighting for possession of a packet of Leopold Schepp's famous dried coconut.

Born and raised on a Michigan farm, Steve Harley (1863-1947) found his artistic expression late in life in the magnificent scenery of the Pacific Northwest.
Harley never married and remained on the Midwest farm through both his parents' lifetimes. After their deaths, Harley became restless and hostile to the confining farm lifestyle. In the mid-1920s, he set off to visit relatives in California and explore the Pacific Northwest. This landscape enthralled Harley, and he made it the subject of four of his five known oll paintings, all of which are owned by the museum along with his sketchbook and photographs.
Apparently the environment also empowered him; on the back of this painting, he described himself as invincible.

Piece Title: Boone's Knoll on the Kentucky River at Camp Nelson
Plaque Description:
Englishman George Beck was one of the first landscapists to cross the Allegheny Mountains. Immigrating to America in 1795, he lived temporarily in Baltimore and Philadelphia. In 1797, George Washington purchased two of Beck's large landscapes for the New Room at Mount Vernon. In 1804, Beck began a painting excursion along the western frontier, drawn by the rumored beauty of the Backcountry. He settled permanently at Lexington, Kentucky, in
1807. Upon his 1812 death, the Kentucky Gazette opined that Beck's
"eminence in landscape painting may rank him amongst the best painters of wild nature."
This scene and three others by Beck were likely acquired by Major William Dallan and Letitia Meredith shortly after their 1808 marriage.
The paintings hung at Winton, the Dallans' Lexington-area home, until the 1960s.

Bankruptcy in the sail cloth business forced 27-year-old John Brand to leave his native Scotland. In 1802, he settled in Lexington, Kentucky, and established a hemp manufactory. National demand for hemp products such as bags and rope helped the business grow. This financial success enabled Brand to return to Scotland and repay old debts nearly 15 years later, an act that earned him a reputation on both sides of the ocean as a "rare - and honest man."
Brand was a major stockholder in the Lexington and Ohio Railroad, a charter board member of the local bank and cemetery, and a close friend and supporter of Henry Clay. He died at age 74, leaving an estate valued today at nearly $18 million dollars. His portrait was rendered by the celebrated local artist Matthew Harris Jouett and was likely accompanied by a companion painting of his wife.

This charming likeness of Félicie Aime was probably painted in conjunction with at least seven other family portraits by this artist. They portray Félicie's parents and four siblings. All were likely rendered around 1839 at completion of the family home, a sixteen-room Greek Revival mansion with extensive gardens nicknamed "Le Petit Versailles" because of its opulence.
The portrait resembles two others by French-born artist Jacques Amans. All feature young women in similar dress and pose against a landscape. Félicie was born to Francois Gabriel and Joséphine Roman Aime, both descended from prominent Louisiana families. Her father was credited as the leading sugar producer in the world and is often called the "father of white sugar."

As a young boy, Washington Bogart Cooper reportedly sketched people on the sides of fences and buildings at his parent's Tennessee farm. According to family history, he later received brief instruction from local artist Ralph E. W. Earl, but probably most impactful was an 1830 trip to Philadelphia, where he studied with Thomas Sully and Henry Inman. Upon Cooper's return home, he established a studio in Nashville and charged $100-150 for a standard bust-length portrait. He would become the state's most prolific painter.
Cooper's rendering of Margery Settle was done about the time of her marriage. Her husband Leroy was a successful businessman in Lebanon, where he was part owner of a hemp factory and a principal in a textile manufactory. The portrait of Margery and a companion likeness of her husband, both in their original frames, remained in the family until recently.

Piece Title: Francina Elizabeth Cox Greer and Daughter Elizabeth Mentoria
Plaque Description: None

Orphaned eleven-year-old John Toole immigrated from his native Ireland to Charlottesville, Virginia, in
1827. Apparently self-taught, the teenaged Toole was painting portraits professionally by the early 1830s. His letters and diaries record the trials and tribulations of itinerant work, as well as the scope of his travels, from Martinsburg in northern West Virginia to Petersburg in southern Virginia.
Toole's papers also confirm that he painted multiple members of the Twyman family in Madison County, Virginia. William Twyman was born there in 1811, and later attended the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. Returning home, he worked as a physician until his death in 1876. Toole alludes to Twyman's profession by including a wooden case of physicians' instruments in this composition

These likenesses of Hanover County tavern owners Daniel and Mary Trueheart portray them with a few tools of their trade: clay tobacco pipes, wine decanter and glasses, jelly (or food) molds, and a brass horn.
Inclusion of the Virginia Gazette in Daniel's hand is notable - its 1794 date represents the year of his son's marriage and likely the date the paintings were produced.
London-born William Hodgson moved to Virginia in
1788. Working in Richmond, he produced architectural
carvings for the new state Capitol and ornamental work for a local cabinetmaker. Recent research has shown that he also painted portraits of several large family groups in adjacent counties, including that of Archer Payne, Sr. Long unidentified, Hodgson was thus known as the Payne Limner. Some two dozen portraits and landscapes are now attributed to his hand.

The son of a Prussian court goldsmith, John Valentine Haidt left metalworking mid-career after a profound religious experience prompted him to join the
Moravian church and become a lay preacher. He soon found that painting portraits and religious scenes within the Moravian community was his true calling. Conflicted, he sought approval from the bishop, Count Nicholas von Zinzendorf. It was likely then that he met the leader's son, Christian von Zinzendorf.

Born in Massachusetts, Ralph Earl trained in England before establishing himself in New York City around 1785. Soon afterward he was sued for nonpayment of a loan and imprisoned for debt in City Hall, the epicenter of local political and judicial life. Yet prison time was beneficial to Earl's career, resulting in 20 portrait commissions and connections that would later yield even more work.
Hailing from St. Helena, South Carolina, William Capers traveled to Fairfield, Connecticut, in 1784 to attend the Rev. Timothy Dwight's school. While there, he met Abigail Burr, a student in the female academy adjacent to Dwight's school for "boys intended for Yale." They were married in 1789 and shortly relocated to South Carolina. Produced in 1788, William's portrait likely hung in the couple's South Carolina home.

These images of James (left and Charlotte Pepper Gignilliat (above) were painted by Philadelphia native Henry Benbridge, one of the few American artists to study in Italy and England before the Revolution.
He settled in Charleston on his return from Europe and there depicted many well-to-do subjects in the restrained settings and informal poses then popular on the Continent. This is particularly evident in the likeness of Charlotte Gignilliat, shown in avant-garde neoclassical "portrait dress." The garments were likely the artist's creation, inspired by Europe's fascination with the classical world.
Married in 1766, the Gignilliats settled in South Carolina's Beaufort district. After the war they relocated to Contentment, a rice plantation near Darien, Georgia.
Their portraits survive in frames likely made in Charleston during the early 19th century.
None

This portrait of teenaged Elizabeth Allen was likely painted in conjunction with her engagement to Scottish merchant and planter John Deas. It is the work of Swiss-born Jeremiah Theus, who recorded an impressive number of Lowcountry subjects between 1740 and his death in 1774. This painting survives in its original imported British frame.
Elizabeth's inherited wealth and John's success allowed them to follow the lead of other well-heeled Carolinians by traveling to Europe. After three years abroad, they returned in 1772 with an array of costly goods, including an Allan Ramsay portrait of John's father. The finest surviving Charleston-made double chest of drawers (at far right) also was among their possessions.

Depictions of enslaved African-Americans are rare, particularly images that lack the distortions of stereotyping. This portrait is unusually empathetic. Mary Custis was the only surviving child of George Washington Parke Custis of Arlington Plantation on the Potomac River. Likely the subject was one of the Custis slaves, though her name is unknown. A minimal setting and skillfully executed details focus attention on the subject, whose quiet dignity dominates the image. Although small, young, and vulnerable, every detail of the girl's attitude conveys self-possession and assurance.
Mary Custis harbored a lifelong concern for the education of slaves, teaching those at Arlington to read and write. Her goal was to prepare them for eventual emancipation.
Her father's will directed that his slaves be freed within five years of his death if his estate were solvent.

Portraits of the wealthy are common in this period, but early images of American craftsmen and women are rare in the extreme. This important likeness depicts William King, Jr., a successful Washington cabinetmaker whose clients included the Monroe White House. Painted in 1841, it marks the occasion of King's 70th birthday and illustrates the tradesman seated in a chair that is likely of his own design. The cherry and maple frame, too, appears to be from the artisan's shop,
The artist, James Alexander Simpson, was a member of the art faculty at nearby Georgetown College (now Georgetown University) and a well-known local portraitist. His portrait of King descended in the subject's family until 2015. It joins several important pieces from the King shop in Colonial Williamsburg's collection.

William Gwathmey was a planter, physician, and trustee of Beulah Baptist Church in King William County, Virginia.
He married Elizabeth Burnley in 1826 and they moved to Burlington Plantation on the Mattaponi River in 1839. They greatly expanded the 18th-century house in 1842, and many of their possessions remained in situ until 1988.
The property also retains an early barn that served as the original meetinghouse for Beulah Baptist Church. Willam's 1830s diaries record the couple's uncommon travels to St.
Augustine, Florida, New Orleans, and Chicago, among other locales.
In 1836, the Gwathmeys commissioned Fredericksburg-area artist William Henry Fairfax to paint these portraits. Fairfax had exhibited at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts in 1834, where he likely met Philadelphia frame maker Frederick
C. Garbanati, whose label marks the back of William's
likeness.

In 1834, art historian William Dunlap wrote that John Durand's portraits were "strong likenesses." The observation is clearly
illustrated in Durand's 1780 rendering of Lucy Skelton Gilliam. Durand depicted striking features-a long neck, high cheekbones, and a prominent jawline. These unusual qualities are infrequently seen in his other works, suggesting that Durand created a true depiction of his subject. On the other hand, the pose, including the closed fan, is typical of 18th-century women's portraiture and was used by several artists from about 1755-1785.
Lucy was the daughter of James Skelton and Jane Meriwether Skelton, both from Tidewater Virginia families. In 1760, she married Robert Gilliam of Prince George County on the James River. The Skeltons and Meriwethers were descendants of distinguished families in England.

Philadelphia clients enjoyed displaying
more
openly. As an example, Harrison wears a miniature portrait on a ribbon around his neck, but the costly object is only half visible, tucked beneath the edge of his waistcoat. Similarly, Harrison is depicted in an expensive but plain suit of blue velvet devoid of superfluous trimmings. Indeed, restraint and elegance characterize every aspect of Peale's sensitive likeness.
The setting is Brandon, Harrison's plantation on the south side of the James River in Prince George County, Virginia. The subject was a member of the State Council in 1776 and the House of Delegates from 1777.

Gilbert Stuart created 12 to 16 versions of this likeness of George Washington, all derived from a life portrait that Stuart later destroyed as unsatisfactory. This example was commissioned from Stuart by Major General Henry ("Light Horse Harry") Lee, a close friend of Washington's and one of the commander-in-chief's most highly-regarded officers during the Revolution. Lee hung the portrait at his Stratford Hall Plantation in Westmoreland County, Virginia.
By the time Washington posed for Stuart in 1795, he had been elected president twice. In modern terms, he had attained cult status, and likenesses of him were in great demand. Stuart was happy to supply them to customers in the South and elsewhere.

John Custis IV was a prominent and powerful Virginia planter who lived on the Eastern Shore and in Williamsburg. In addition to managing his multiple plantations, he sat on the Virginia Governor's Council. Like many of the Virginia gentry, Custis furnished his house with an array of imported goods. In addition to the atlas seen below, he ordered a variety of furniture forms, paintings, prints, textiles, and glassware from his London merchant. Custis took most pride, however, in his expansive gardens and repeatedly requested that his agent send bulbs for double tulips. Artist Charles Bridges captured Custis's love for horticulture by painting the book in his left hand, Of The Tulip, accompanied by the cut flower.
Bridges was English-born and served Virginia as the colony's first documented professional portraitist.

British-trained artist John Wollaston Jr. came to America in 1749, bringing with him an understanding of painting styles recently made popular in London. His use of fashionable poses, colors, expressions, and costume in his portraits was well-received by wealthy Americans. During Wollaston's brief stay in Virginia, he painted over 100 portraits, the largest number by any artist there before 1800.
Wollaston's portrait of Frances Ann Tasker Carter was likely created around the time of her marriage to Robert Carter III and probably served as a companion to an earlier English portrait of her husband. A glowing description of Frances Carter can be found in the diary of Philip Vickers Fithian, tutor in the Carter household. The Carters lived at Nomini Hall in Westmoreland County, Virginia,
except for a period of nearly a
decade. Between the years 1761 and 1772, the couple resided with their family at the house on Palace
Green
in Williamsburg now
known as the Robert Carter House.

From 1689 until his death in 1723, Sir Godfrey Kneller served as principal painter to the king. In that capacity, he was responsible for official state portraits of the monarch. Yet much of his time was consumed by private commissions from those who aspired to political, economic, and social success.
William Byrd II inherited great estates in Virginia which, together with the force of his personality and his own accomplishments, made him one of the most prominent and powerful men in the colony. His stylish portrait is an example of his ambitions, having been painted in London by the most prestigious studio of the day.
Byrd brought his portrait back to Virginia to hang at Westover, the manor house on his Charles City County plantation. Over the ensuing years, he amplified the painting's impact and further emulated the English elite by assembling and displaying a collection of more than 30 portraits of family members and friends, an extraordinary cultural achievement for the time and place.

Frances Parke Custis (called Fanny was the daughter of John Custis IV, among the wealthiest Virginians of his day. Depicted in her early teens, Fanny's loosely arranged attire is likely based on printed images of British noblewomen and may be more fanciful than accurate. The roses are a reference to her young womanhood. In the Chesapeake and elsewhere, a costly portrait was often intended as a statement about the subject's status, taste, and gender role.
The likeness was painted by an unidentified artist who produced a number of portraits in the 1720s for the Brodnax and Jaquelin families of Jamestown and Williamsburg. Known today as the Jaquelin-Brodnax Limner, his other surviving works are bust-length; this is the only known three-quarter length canvas. The imported British frame may be original to the painting.

Charles Bridges arrived in Virginia in the mid-1730s and quickly earned the patronage of the leading Tidewater families. Over the course of about eight years, he painted portraits for many of the colony's wealthiest residents, depicting them as confident, fashionably dressed citizens of a larger British society.
Tradition suggests that this young sitter was a member of the Ludwell family of Greensprings Plantation near Williamsburg.
The Ludwells held prominent roles in local government and at the College of William and Mary. They occupied their estate for over 100 years, witnessing numerous historic events including occupation by American forces under the command of the Marquis de Lafayette during the Revolutionary War.
The portrait survives in its original English frame. When new, the carved surface was silvered rather than gilded.

Likely born in Britain, William Dering arrived in Virginia in 1737. He lived in rural Gloucester County before moving to Williamsburg, where he worked as a dancing master and portrait painter. Dering enjoyed connections to the colony's elite, regularly interacting with the Byrds, Carters, Randolphs, and their peers.
Joyce Armistead Booth was the matriarch of a wealthy Gloucester family. Her uncommonly large, visually commanding, and well-preserved portrait is among Dering's finest efforts. Its scale and colorful composition were meant to impress viewers and convey Mrs. Booth's taste and status.
William Dering produced an equally impressive portrait of Mrs. Booth's teenaged son, George, in which he is flanked by life size marble sculptures.
Such unusual compositions may have been inspired by the more than 200 prints in
Dering's possession.

José Salazar was born in Mérida on Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula and immigrated to Spanish-held New Orleans in
1782. Once established in that bustling, cosmopolitan port, the artist quickly made a name for himself portraying its leading figures. Salazar would dominate portraiture in New Orleans for 20 years until his death in 1802.
William Preston Smith was born in Kentucky about 1780.
At the age of 14 he was appointed an ensign in America's fledgling army, The Legion of the United States. In 1797 he was promoted to lieutenant and on March 21, 1800, he gained the rank of captain while serving in New Orleans.
Sadly, he died there just over a year later, probably of yellow fever.
In Salazar's likeness of Smith, the single epaullette on his right shoulder signifies his new captaincy.

Col. Isaac Barré served in North America
during the French and Indian War. On returning home, he was elected to Parliament, where his vigorous opposition to the taxation of the colonies garnered deep admiration in America. In a notable speech delivered to Parliament in 1765, Barré originated the description of American patriots as the "Sons of Liberty," The next year Sir Joshua Reynolds depicted Barré pointing to a map of North America, emphasizing his political convictions.
Reynolds was among the most gifted artists of the 18th century. He was also a founding member of the Royal Academy, an institution established in 1768 by King George III to provide professional training for artists in Britain.

These prints, drawn and engraved by Thomas
Frye, are part of a series illustrating fashionably dressed subjects. They are among the finest examples of the mezzotint engraving process.
The sensitivity and expressiveness of the sitters was achieved through Frye's manipulation of light and dark tones and enabled him to capture a specific moment in the lives of his subjects.

Bartholomew Dandridge was born in nearby New Kent County, Virginia, in 1773 or 1774.
He spent much of his childhood in Williamsburg, where his father, Bartholomew senior, owned the Elizabeth Carlos House on Waller Street. The elder Dandridge was a younger brother of Martha Dandridge Custis Washington. Young Bartholomew
was
consequently George Washington's nephew by marriage and served as his private secretary from 1791 until 1797. In the latter year,
Oil on canvas
Museum Purchase, 1973-198
Dandridge traveled to London to serve as secretary to Rufus King, minister plenipotentiary to Great Britain.
While in London, Dandridge sat for this striking portrait, executed by his countryman, John Trumbull. Although best known as a history painter, Trumbull performed many roles including teacher, architect, cartographer, soldier, and diplomat.

Born into a wealthy Virginia family, Daniel Parke's political and military aspirations led him to England as a young man. He found fame at the conclusion of the 1704 Battle of Blenheim in Germany. Handsome and popular, Parke was chosen by the Duke of Marlborough to carry word of England's victory back to Queen Anne. Elated by the news, she presented Parke with a miniature portrait of herself, which appears on a ribbon around his neck in this painting
and all other known likenesses of him.
Sir Godfrey Kneller depicted Parke heroically dressed in field armor, holding the baton of command, and with the Battle of Blenheim raging in the background. The gifted Kneller was one of England's leading portrait painters during the late 17th and early 18th centuries. He served as court painter to both Charles II and George I.

As a prominent Dutch political leader, William of Orange invaded England in 1688, successfully dethroning his Catholic uncle and father-in-law, King James II, and restoring Protestantism to the British Crown. Together with his wife, Mary, he established the first joint English monarchy. During their reign, the couple granted a charter for the College of William and Mary in 1693 and William became the namesake of the city of Williamsburg upon its establishment in 1699.
William II's likeness portrays him in his royal regalia and is one of many copies that functioned as the official image of the King for private and public spaces both in England and abroad. He was painted by the studio of Sir Godfrey Kneller, principal painter to William and Mary. The frame is a hand-carved, silver-gilt reproduction based on period profiles.
None

Piece Title: Portrait of Ellin North Moale and her Granddaughter Ellin North Moale
Plaque Description:
Joshua Johnson, one of America's first Black professional artists, worked in the Baltimore area for 30 years beginning about 1795. Born into slavery, he was freed in
1782. Little is known of Johnson's career path, but he once referenced "having experienced many insuperable obstacles in the pursuit of his studies."
With its complex background and costuming, Johnson's likeness of Ellin Moale and her namesake granddaughter is one of his most ambitious. Moale sat for several academically trained artists over the years, including John Hesselius, John Wollaston, Jr., and Rembrandt Peale.
Her decision to sit for Johnson may have been due to the fact that they were near neighbors. Notably, Moale's husband, Justice John Moale, signed Johnson's manumission papers.

Clementine Hunter often recorded scenes from her life on
and around Melrose Plantation,
where she lived and worked for most of her life. This piece depicts several of the buildings from the estate as well as tasks that Hunter was involved in, such as harvesting crops and doing laundry.
Of particular importance to Hunter's story is the African House pictured at the top of her
painting. The African House was built around 1815, but its original use is unclear. In the summer of 1955, Hunter spent seven weeks painting autobiographical murals around the entire second floor. The buildings featured in her murals are also found in this work, including the sundial, depicted in the upper left corner here.
This armillary sphere is seen in many of Hunter's Melose paintings and was supposedly how
Hunter learned to tell time.

Born in 1887, Clementine Hunter spent most of her life working in the fields and kitchen at Melrose Plantation in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana. She spoke only Creole French until she was nearly 40 and could neither read nor write. During its heyday, Melrose was a center for arts, history, and culture, inspiring artists and writers to visit and stay at the property. Hunter's first painting was created on a window shade with discarded paint left by one of the guests.
For nearly 40 years, Hunter painted the people in her community and activities of daily life in and around the plantation, like this one depicting an outdoor baptism. Of her work, she simply remarked, "I tell my stories by marking pictures," "My art is a gift from the Lord." Her joyful and vibrant depictions show that despite many hardships, she lived a full life around the people and places she loved.

Jimmy Lee Sudduth was only a toddler when he created his first picture-a dog drawn with mud smeared across the top of a tree stump near his rural Alabama home. When the image washed away, he became determined to find a method that kept the mud in place, leading him to develop his signature "sweet mud," a combination of dirt, water, and various syrups. Sudduth incorporated both natural materials and household goods in his work including berries, grasses, coffee grounds, axle grease, and leftover house paint. While his choice to render this enlarged hundred-dollar bill is unusual, the technique of using his fingers to paint is typical of Sudduth's work.

Mose Tolliver, his wife, and their large family lived in Montgomery, Alabama. While employed at a furniture factory in the late 1960s, a serious workplace accident left him physically disabled. Soon Tolliver began to create art using house paint, plywood, poster board, and other found materials, all in a distinctive style. His paintings often featured colorful birds, large animals, and trees, but in the self-portrait seen here he documented a painful personal reality: that after the injury, he could neither stand nor walk without assistance.

Piece Title: Big Daddy's House at Hickory Hill
Plaque Description:
Bernice Sims came to art late in life after surgery left her unable to work. To stay busy, she enrolled in community college art classes and explored her long-held interest in painting. A chance meeting with noted Black artist Mose Tolliver, who lived nearby, spurred her on.
Many of Sims's works, including this one, reflect her memories of rural childhood and family activities. Others depict her role as an early civil rights activist. In 2005, the U.S.
Postal Service honored Sims with a stamp featuring her painting of the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, scene of 1965's Selma-to-Montgomery march, in which she participated.

Born into slavery near Benton, Alabama, Bill Traylor remained on the property of his former enslaver, George Traylor (from whom the artist took his surname following emancipation. In 1938, he moved to Montgomery and began producing paintings and drawings, eventually creating some 1,500 to 1,800 artworks.
Traylor's extraordinary body of work is both abstract and figurative. His innate sense of form and placement and his concise conveyance of mood imbue his paintings and drawings with clarity, wit, and grace.

Piece Title: Portrait of Susanna Cardwell McCausland and Child
Plaque Description:
Joshua Johnson is one of America's earliest documented Black professional artists. Born into slavery about 1763, he was manumitted at the age of 19 after completing an apprenticeship in blacksmithing. Johnson instead pursued a career as a portraitist, later describing himself as "self-taught." Only two of the known portraits from his
30-year career depict Black subjects; the rest portray middle class and wealthy white citizens of Baltimore and its vicinity. Shown here is Susanna McCausland, who immigrated from Ireland to Maryland in 1804. On her lap is one of her ten known children.

Piece Title: Woman in Green Hat and Yellow Coat
Plaque Description:
Born in 1915, Anderson Johnson became a street preacher at the age of eight after receiving a message from God. Later in life, a medical bill he could not pay, and a divine inspiration encouraged him to begin painting.
Johnson collected small fees for his art to help maintain his ministry. In the early 1970s, he began transforming his home into a "faith mission" where he conducted services every Sunday. Johnson covered the interior with paintings and inscriptions, some executed directly on the walls. Occasionally he painted members of his church; this portrait may be one of them.

Piece Title: Untitled (Brown and Black Figure with Yellow)
Plaque Description:
Mary Smith began painting when she was nearly 70, but images had filled her mind throughout her life. As a child, she suffered from a severe hearing loss that isolated her but also made her intensely independent.
Having her own home later in life allowed Smith to explore her imagination in a new way. She transformed the house and garden into an artistic environment with bold paintings on plywood or corrugated tin, some incorporating text, and many worked in only two or three colors. Some of Smith's images seem to draw inspiration from West African ceremonial masks, while others sprang from her Christian faith. Displaying her art in this way finally allowed Smith to express herself to the world.

Richard Burnside began painting after a foot injury sidelined his short stint in the military.
He discovered that art distracted him from pain but also provided pleasure for himself and others. Much of Burnside's adult life was spent in Pendleton, South Carolina, where he worked in jobs ranging from store clerk to restaurant chef. Later in life, he painted in Pendleton's downtown square where he loved to see people enjoying his art.
Burnside's work often included Africanized mask-like faces that he called Kings and Queens.
These figures usually incorporated heavy outlines, dot patterns, and bright colors. Burnside said his Kings and Queens symbolized authority and power, but he also painted them simply because people liked them.

Piece Title: Captain Thomas Trent Jr and William Henry Trent
Plaque Description:
This portrait of Captain Thomas Trent, Jr. and his son, William, was painted by Samuel Taylor. At the time, Taylor also painted the companion portrait of Trent's wife, Martha, and their daughter, Joella. The family lived in Buckingham (now Appomattox)
County, Virginia, on an estate called Rural View.
Samuel Taylor worked in the Virginia Piedmont between
Richmond and Lynchburg from 1825 to 1845. The qualities of his work suggest he had no formal artistic training.
Nevertheless, his use of
symbolic props such as the books in this portrait was based on an understanding of common artistic conventions. Like other rural artists, Taylor found his clients through word of mouth between his sitters' relations and neighbors. That is likely the case with Trent, whose relatives were also portrayed by Taylor.
None

When 17-year-old Adam Stephen Dandridge, Jr. had his portrait painted by artist James Macoughtry (1808-1841), he was likely a student at Princeton.
After his graduation in 1833, Dandridge returned home to Jefferson County, Virginia (now West Virginia), where he became prominent in local and Virginia politics.
Macoughtry, a fellow resident Jefferson County, attended the Philadelphia Academy of Art while in his teens and visited with noted artist Thomas Sully. Macoughtry seems to
have been influenced not only by Sully, but also
by artist
Philip
Tilyard, who painted Dandridge's first cousin, John Pendleton Kennedy in
1827. Copying the Tilyard painting allowed Macoughtry to practice his style and technique. A receipt dated 1831, records payment of $60 to Macoughtry for two portraits, this one of young Dandridge and another of
his mother. A year later, through the
generosity of another satisfied client,
Macoughtry travelled abroad to continue his training.

Brothers Stevens Thomson Mason and John Thomson Mason were grandnephews of Revolutionary War patriot George Mason. They were also cousins of John Mason, Jr., whose wife's portrait by Thomas Sully hangs nearby. John Thomson Mason studied at the College of William and Mary and married Elizabeth Moir in Williamsburg in 1809 before moving to Kentucky. Younger brother Stevens died at the age of 26.
These portraits were painted by French artist Francis Cezeron during a visit to Virginia. Foreign-born artists saw American travel as an economic opportunity. Little is known about Cezeron's training, but newspaper advertisements mark his arrival in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, as a dance instructor and French teacher. The
first reference to portrait painting appears in 1809 in Frederick, Maryland 2. Over the next decade, he traveled to Carlisle and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Culpeper County, Fredericksburg, and Loudoun County, Virginia. His profile portraits of the Masons bear similarities to the early work of fellow Lancaster resident and
painter Jacob Eichholtz, who may have been trained by Cezeron.
None

Originally from Philadelphia, Dr. Elisha Hall lived in Fredericksburg, Virginia, where his patients included George Washington's mother, Mary Ball Washington.
Hall and noted Philadelphia physician Benjamin Rush were first cousins. In 1789, Hall sought Rush's advice on treatment for Mrs. Washington's breast cancer. Rush wrote that "there does not exist in the vegetable kingdom an antidote to cancers." Mrs.
Washington died a month later.
Charles Peale Polk painted these portraits of Hall and his wife, Caroleana Carter Hall,
around 1795. Mrs. Hall's portrait was clearly inspired by the likeness of Rush's wife, Julia Stockton Rush. Mrs.
Rush was depicted by Polk's uncle, mentor, and painting teacher, Charles Willson Peale, in 1776. At that time, the younger artist lived with his uncle and learned the rudiments of the painting trade.
None

Little is known about Amos Morrow, but he apparently had no problem being captured for posterity as he really was, scalp tumors and all. Artist Charles Peale Polk needed to please his client in order to get paid, so Morrow must have been satisfied with the final image. In addition to Amos Morrow, Polk painted portraits of Amos' wife, Matilda, and the couple's two daughters.
The training Polk received from his famous uncle, Trenes are The See Be ad stan set to
likenesses. The swagged red curtain used as a backdrop and the oval framing appear in many of Polk's pictures. He drew upon his experience in the Peale household for the multiple commissions he received throughout the western areas of Virginia and Maryland, including his time with the Morrows in Jefferson County, Virginia (now West Virginia).
None

Peter Lenox, son of a Williamsburg wigmaker and barber, had a hand in the most iconic buildings in our nation's capital: the White House and the Capitol. Drawing on associations likely made during apprenticeships with two Richmond, Virginia, joiners, he eventually secured federal appointments as carpenter and builder. This portrait by Charles Bird King displays some of the drawing instruments Lenox used in his work.
A sizable inheritance enabled
Rhode Island native king to apprentice in New York
with artist Edward Savage before traveling to London to study with artist Benjamin West.
King returned in 1812, settling in Philadelphia.
After a period of itinerancy, he moved
to Washington, D.C., where he painted these portraits of Peter and Margaret Lenox. King is best known today for a series of 143 portraits of Native
Americans painted between 1821 and 1842.

Piece Title: Margaret Welling Lenox and Walter Lenox
Plaque Description: None

Here Thomas Sully captured the love of first-time mother Catherine Macomb Mason for her year-old son, John _ Henry. Catherine and her husband, John Mason Jr., lived in Georgetown, D. C. A noted politician and lawyer, John was the grandson of George Mason, author of the Virginia Declaration of Rights (which later served as the basis for the U.S. Bill of Rights).
Catherine and John married in 1827 and John Henry was born a year later, the first of 10 children. Sadly four of them died very young, including John Henry, who passed away two years after posing with his mother for this portrait.

In a journal entry for June 1st, 1829, Thomas Sully noted that he
"began Mrs. Mason and Child."
Nearly two months later, he completed the portrait along with a likeness of Catherine's father, Major General
Alexander Macomb, hero of the War of 1812 and Commander and Chief of the United States Army at West Point.
None

Elizabeth “Eliza” Jameson stands out in this exhibition as the only sitter to be decked out in gold jewelry, From her filligree and paste earrings to the pocket watch at her waist, she presents quite a picture as a 28-year-old wife and mother. The music book in her hand hints at her interest in a subject learned by most fashionable young women of the period.
Over the course of 1831-1832, Eliza's parents, William and Elizabeth Major, commissioned Thomas Jefferson Wright to paint portraits of themselves and at least eight members of their immediate family, including Eliza. These portraits, as well as others the artist completed in Culpeper County, Virginia, may be the earliest works by Wright after he received formal training, possibly in Philadelphia.
They demonstrate a stylistic change from his earlier works, like the portraits of the Howards to the left

These portraits of dry goods merchant George Howard and his wife, Cassandra Hukill Howard, are among Thomas Jefferson Wright's earliest known works. The Howards took to the young artist and made arrangements for him to meet celebrated local artist, Matthew Harris Jouett, who himself wrote a letter of introduction to Thomas Sully for Wright in 1822. How much of a role the Howards played in Wright's artistic career is yet to be determined, but a portrait of their son, Thomas Gibson Howard, was painted by Wright in 1833, suggesting the couple stayed in touch with the young artist.
Unframing the portrait the allowed protected area of the painted surface to be seen. This area revealed that Cassandra's dress was a vibrant rose-violet color, making
it evident that much of the visible dress had faded over time. This digital re-colorization, based upon this well-preserved portion of the
painting, helps us see her as the artist originally intended.

Selfies are made at the click of a button today, but creating a self-portrait in the 19th century required both patience and artistic ability. Self-portraits by untrained artists are rare,
The third painting that I ever
and several features make this one by John Stevenson extraordinary. An inscription on the back (right) is signed by the artist.
Stevenson was born at Newtown (now Pocomoke City) on the Eastern Shore of Maryland. At a young age, he went to Baltimore to learn silversmithing from Samuel Kirk, then to New York City to study watchmaking. At 20, he settled
in Snow Hill, Maryland. Over the course of his lifetime, Stevenson was also a merchant, a farmer, and a postmaster. He engraved, sketched, cut silhouettes, painted political banners and portraits, and fashioned furniture as well. Their daughter described Harriet "as a woman of excellent judgement... She was a close observer and had a remarkable ability to judge character"
None

Yes, these are the same subject by the same artist, Cephas Thompson. Today we think nothing of printing multiple photographic portraits, but we don't expect to find original portraits that look so alike unless one is a copy or even a forgery. That is not the case here. The Williamsons commissioned at least five portraits of themselves from Thompson, most likely as gifts for family members. The couple had at least eight children together and three from Thomas' first marriage.

A banker and local politician, Thomas Williamson considered himself a patron of the arts. In addition to Thompson, the Williamsons patronized other American artists, including
William James Hubard and William Dunlap, the noted artist-diarist who described in an 1819 visit to the couple seeing multiple landscapes, copies, and "some dozen" portraits by Thompson.
A register of the artist's Norfolk subjects, presumably written in the order that they were painted, lists the canvas of "Mrs. Williamson" before the smaller panel picture. The dramatic artist's changes in the subject's drape and the contour lines of her figure, seen only in the canvas under a microscope, also suggest the larger format was the earlier likeness.
